title: Analysis: measuring combos, movement and how the hunt goes
tagline: Offline instruments that measure recordings and telemetry; they never decide anything
summary: The analysis layer is gamelab's measuring kit. It records short clips of the game with the keys sent and follows her name tag through them to judge combos and compare her movement with the physics models, and it reads the hunt's telemetry to say how route moves are used, how soon platforms refill, what jump attacks achieve and how her real walk compares with the planned one. A few tools time and check perception on saved frames; almost everything runs offline and sends no keys.
details_md:
The analysis layer is gamelab's set of measuring instruments. It never decides anything the hunt does: every module
reads evidence and prints a table, and almost all of it runs offline with no game and no keys. It may import
`perception`, `motion`, `control` and the shared modules only (`tests/test_architecture.py`), which is why some of
its inputs (the map model, the camera's model, the shooting band) are handed in by the command that calls it rather
than loaded here.

**Two kinds of evidence.**

- **Recordings.** A short capture of the game window with the keys sent: `recordings.record` hands a key timeline to
  the elevated key player through `control.client.submit`, and keeps the frames, their times and the keys planned
  and actually sent as `lab/recordings/<name>.npz` plus `<name>.events.json`. The rolling recorder and the Lie
  Detector recorder (in `control`) keep a different kind: folders of JPEG frames with an `index.jsonl`, which
  `recordings.Folder` reads into contact sheets and real-time mp4s.
- **Telemetry.** Every hunt, tour, probe, `watch` and simulated run writes JSON-lines records to `lab/telemetry/`
  (`scene`, `route`, `chain`, `moved`, `trip`, `jump`, `event`, ...). The perception service writes its own
  `*-perceive.jsonl` beside them, several scene records a second.

**From a recording to numbers.** `calibration` finds her name tag once and keeps a grayscale template and a crop
around her. Each frame of a recording is then matched against that template (`track`, OpenCV `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED`,
optionally to a fifth of a pixel with a parabola through the scores). Because the camera follows her, `scroll`
measures how far the scenery moved (phase correlation of the strip under her, or the median shift of textured
grass and dirt patches) so her movement is read in the world, not on screen. On top of that, `analyze` splits a run
of combos into jumps (back, forward, straight up) and claw throws (toward the front or the wrong way) and checks key
send lag and the game's frame pacing, and `physics_check` compares her tracked path against the motion models as an
RMS error in map units.

**From telemetry to numbers.**

| Module | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| `coverage` | Which route moves are planned, taken, missed; where she spends her time; why the never-taken moves lose |
| `respawn` | How soon a platform she empties has a monster again, how long drops lie, how full platforms are (Kaplan-Meier) |
| `jumps` | What came of each jump attack (kill, hit, nothing seen) and whether the 2026-11-01 key jitter predicts a hit |
| `walkfit` | Her real walk and climb against the walk her moves were planned at; late takeoffs; step ratios; wrong arrivals |
| `bodies` | Where the monster detector puts feet; how much monster x jitters frame to frame; the feed's track velocities |

**Checking perception offline.** `bench` times every stage of a look on saved screenshots (through `SavedEyes`,
the real `Eyes` with its captures replaced) or live without touching the window. `pasted` draws the game's own
monster and drop sprites onto 1366x768 frames, alpha-blended as the game draws them, at known places, and measures
how many the detectors find and how far off. `disk` sizes what `gamelab/lab` holds.

**Screen geometry.** The pixel constants here were measured on the 1920x1080 window: a few in its client (screen)
px (the calibration crop, `TAG_SLACK`), most in its half-size look frames (the jump lift, the claw-swing box, the
scroll patches, `bodies.LINK_PX`). Since 2026-10-23 the game also runs at its own 1366x768, shown full size, so the
modules convert them with `screen.Geometry` (`px`/`ipx` for screen px, `fpx`/`ifpx` for look-frame px), and a
recording keeps its own client size and scale (one saved before 2026-10-23 is the 1920x1080 window at half size).

**Who uses it.** `gamelab/__main__.py` wires the commands: `calibrate`, `snap`, `act`, `do`, `combo`, `lock`,
`sheet`, `track`, `check` (recordings and calibration), `bench-look`, `bench-capture`, `bench-paste`, `bodies`
(perception checks), `coverage`, `jitter`, `respawn` (telemetry) and `lab-usage` (`save-recent` borrows
`disk.size`). `walkfit` and `physics_check` have no `gamelab` command: they run only as
`python -m gamelab.analysis.walkfit` / `.physics_check`; `jumps` also prints its own outcome table as
`python -m gamelab.analysis.jumps`, besides the `jitter` command. The simulator harness keeps a
`coverage.tally` of every run, `sim.soak` and `sim.replay_run` use `bench.SavedEyes` and `calibration.load`, and
`sim.fakes` replaces `recordings.record` with a refusal so a simulated run can never record the real game.

**Design habits.** Reports state their denominators ("12 of 77 seen back"), censor what wasn't watched instead of
guessing, and say where an outcome comes from: in the simulator a pattern is the simulator's own model, so live runs
are where results mean something.

modules.title: The analysis package
modules.tagline: Package docstring: what analysis measures and which layers it may import
modules.summary: The package's only content is its docstring. It names what the layer is for (recording the game, measuring combos and her movement, the calibration that finds her, route coverage) and its import rule.
modules.details_md:
The docstring says the analysis layer records the game around her and measures combos in the recordings (her path,
jumps, throws, key timing), her movement against the physics models (`physics_check`), the calibration that finds
her on screen, and how her routes' moves are used in the harness's runs and the live telemetry (`coverage`).

It also states the import rule: **analysis may import perception, motion, control and the shared modules**. The
rule is enforced by `tests/test_architecture.py` (`ALLOWED["analysis"] = {"perception", "motion", "control"}`), and
`sim` is allowed to import analysis. This is why `respawn` is handed the camera's corner function and the shooting
band by its command instead of importing `localization.pose.Camera` or `attack.reach`, and why `jumps` copies the
jitter windows from `attack.reach` rather than importing them (a test checks they agree).

The package has no code of its own; nothing is re-exported, so callers import the submodules directly
(`from gamelab.analysis import coverage`).
outputs: the layer's description and import rule, for readers and tests/test_architecture.py
gotchas: Nothing is re-exported: `import gamelab.analysis` alone gives no tools; import each submodule.

modules.title: Recordings
modules.tagline: Record a key timeline with frames, save and load it, and tile frames into sheets
modules.summary: Runs a key timeline through the key player while it captures the game window, and saves the frames, their times and the keys planned and sent under a name in lab/recordings. Also loads them back, makes contact sheets, and reads the JPEG-folder recordings of the rolling and Lie Detector recorders into sheets or real-time videos.
modules.details_md:
**The named recordings.** A `Recording` holds `frames` (an `(n, h, w, 3)` RGB array), `times` (ms relative to the
plan's first key event, so frames before the first key have negative times), `planned` and `sent` key events
(`[ms, key, 'down'|'up']`), and the game window's `client` size and `scale` (how much the frames were shrunk). Its
`geo` property turns the last two into a `screen.Geometry`, which every measuring module uses to convert its pixel
constants.

`record(events, name=, duration_ms=, crop=, scale=, fps=60, lead_ms=100)` caps the frame rate at
`900_000 / (duration_ms + lead_ms)` because the player caps a plan at 900 frames, then calls `control.client.submit`
(which writes the plan to `lab/inbox` and waits for the elevated player's answer in `lab/outbox`). The result's
client area gives the size; problems the player reports are printed. It saves and returns the recording.
`screenshot` is the same path with no keys: a 200 ms capture at 10 fps, its last frame.

`save` writes `lab/recordings/<name>.npz` (compressed `frames` and `times`) and `<name>.events.json`
(`planned`, `sent`, `client`, `scale`). `load` reads both; a recording without its events file gets empty key lists,
and one saved before 2026-10-23 (no `client`/`scale`) is taken as the 1920x1080 window at half size.
`file_geometry(path)` gives that geometry for an `.npz` anywhere (used by `bodies`).

`contact_sheet` tiles every `every`-th frame (default 3) into `cols` columns (default 8), each labelled with its
time in ms (yellow on a black box), optionally zoomed with nearest-neighbour.

**The JPEG-folder recordings.** The rolling recorder (`control.rolling`, the game 10 times a second, kept for
`save-recent` and the part before a Lie Detector) and `control.lie_recorder` write a folder of JPEG frames with an
`index.jsonl`. `load_folder` reads the index into a `Folder`: frames as `(t, file, label)` (label the clock time if
the line has `at`) and gaps as `(t, until, why)`. A line it can't parse (half written when the writer stopped) is
skipped.

- `folder_sheet` picks one frame every `SHEET_EVERY` (10: a second's worth at 10 fps), shrinks each `SHEET_SHRINK`
  (4) times with OpenCV's area average, and tiles them. It reads only the picked frames, because five minutes of
  frames are 9 GB as pictures.
- `folder_video` writes an mp4 that plays in real time at `VIDEO_FPS` (10): each output frame shows the newest
  frame or gap at or before that moment, a gap as a grey card (`GAP_GREY` 40) saying "no frame: <why>", and the
  clock time at the top left. It uses OpenCV's own `mp4v` (MPEG-4 Part 2) because its build has no H.264; the
  docstring says that is about 30 dB, with the HUD's text legible. Frames of another size (the window resized
  mid-recording) are resized to the first's.

modules.title: Calibration
modules.tagline: Find her name tag once, keep its template and the crop recordings take
modules.summary: Finds her name tag on screen, saves a grayscale template of it and a recording crop around her, one calibration per client size and per character. Before every recording it finds her again with that template and moves the crop if she has walked away.
modules.details_md:
Her name tag (white text on a dark box under her feet) is how every recording finds her, so this module keeps the
two things that depend on where and how big it is: **the crop** recordings are taken of, and **the template** that
finds her in them.

**`calibrate(tag=None, fresh=False)`**:

1. Takes a full-size (scale 1) 200 ms capture through the key player that sends no keys, and works out the window's
   `Geometry` from its client size. The recording scale is `geo.look_scale`: 2 at 1920x1080 (half-size frames,
   "plenty for tracking, 4x less data"), 1 at the game's own 1366x768.
2. Saves that frame for checking by eye (`lab/calibrate.png`, `calibrate_1366x768.png` at the game's size; another
   character's under `lab/characters/<id>/`).
3. Unless `fresh`, reuses the saved template (her name tag looks the same on every map) to find her: `match_tag`
   matches it on a copy shrunk `scale` times and accepts a score of `TAG_MATCH_MIN` (0.7) or better. Otherwise
   `track.find_name_tag` takes the name-tag-shaped text nearest the middle. If nothing is found it raises, asking
   for `--tag X,Y`.
4. `crop_around` places an 800x400 client-pixel crop (at 1920x1080; 569x284 at 1366x768) with her tag at
   (400, 300) inside it, leaving room above for jumps, clamped inside the window.
5. Takes a screenshot of that crop at the recording scale, and if the template is new cuts it there with
   `track.make_template` and saves it; the full-size template is then deleted so `perception.nametag` cuts a fresh
   one on its next look.
6. Writes the calibration JSON: crop, scale, tag position and client size.

**Files per size and character.** `files(geo)` returns `paths.calibrated(...)` names: at 1920x1080 the files as
they always were (`lab/calibration.json`, `lab/tag_template.npy`, `lab/tag_template_full.npy`), at other sizes the
same with a `_1366x768` suffix. `paths.of()` puts another character's in her own folder so hers don't overwrite the
thief's.

**Re-finding her before each recording.** `crop_on_her(cal, frame, w, h)` matches the template on a fresh full-size
frame. If her tag is within `TAG_SLACK` (40 client px at 1920x1080, converted) of where calibrate would put it in
the stored crop, the stored crop is kept and nothing is said; otherwise a new crop is made around her and the
caller is told where she is and whether the stored crop still had her. If the tag isn't found, the stored crop is
used with a warning. `crop_now` does this on a 100 ms capture. The reason, from the docstring: on 2026-10-21 the
16 `act --record` runs of a sweep never had her in their crop, because the calibration was from a place she had
walked away from.

`load(geo)` reads the saved calibration for a size and raises "not calibrated at WxH yet" if there is none.

modules.title: Tracking her in recordings
modules.tagline: Follow her name tag frame by frame; spot jumps and claw swings
modules.summary: Follows her through recorded frames by template-matching her name tag, finds name tags without a template, and turns the track into airborne spans (jumps) and claw swings with the side they went. Everything works in the recording's frame pixels, converted by its geometry.
modules.details_md:
A **track** is one row per frame: `(t ms, x, y, match score)`, where `x, y` is the name tag's **top-left corner**
(not its centre). The first row is where she stood when the recording started; jumps are measured against it.

**Finding a name tag without a template** (`_tag_boxes`, `find_name_tag`). Pixels whose smallest channel is over
215 are "white text". The mask is dilated sideways with a 3x13 kernel (`LETTER_GAP`) so a name's letters join into
one blob, then OpenCV's connected components gives boxes. A box is a name tag if it is 25-180 px wide, 8-26 px tall,
at least 2.2 times wider than tall, and the non-white pixels inside it are dark (median of their brightest channel
under 110). Her face, gloves, clouds and other bright scenery fail these checks. `find_name_tag` returns the centre
of the one nearest the middle of the frame, ignoring the bottom tenth (the HUD).

**The template** (`make_template`). From a centre, it takes a band one text line high (12 screen px above and
below, 90 either side, converted by the geometry and divided by the scale), keeps the rows and columns with white
(over 200) pixels, cuts tightly with a 2 px margin and converts to grayscale. The thin band keeps her glove or a
rope out. It raises if there are fewer than `10 // scale` columns of text.

**Matching.** `best_match` runs `cv2.matchTemplate(..., TM_CCOEFF_NORMED)` on the grayscale frame and returns the
top-left and score. `fine_match` refines it to a fraction of a pixel: `peak(a, b, c)` fits a parabola through the
scores one pixel either side of the best and returns `0.5 * (a - c) / (a - 2b + c)` (0 if the curve doesn't peak).
Her tag moves smoothly, so this tracks her to about 0.2 px (0.3 map units in a half-size frame). `track` uses the
whole-pixel match; `physics_check` uses the fine one.

**Jumps** (`airborne`). A frame is "up" when the tag is at least `lift` (6 half-size px of the 1920x1080 window,
converted) above its first-row height. Runs of up frames become `(takeoff, landing)` spans; spans less than
`merge_ms` (60 ms) apart are merged (a mis-match can split one jump in two), and spans shorter than `min_ms`
(150 ms) are dropped (a jump lasts about 530 ms). A span still open at the end has landing `None`.

**Claw swings** (`swing_side`, `swings`). The throw effect is bright white or lavender pixels next to her (both the
regular attack and Lucky Seven). `_bright` counts pixels whose smallest channel is over 170 and whose blue is at
least their green, in a box `SWING_SIDE` (70) px wide on each side of the tag, from `SWING_ABOVE` (45) px above it
to 2 px above. The baseline is the largest count before the first key (frames with t < 0). A frame is a swing frame
if left+right exceeds that baseline by `SWING_MIN_PIXELS` (40, scaled by the square of the px conversion). Swing
frames closer than `BURST_GAP_MS` (150 ms) are one swing; its side is whichever count was larger in the burst's
strongest frame.

modules.title: Camera scroll
modules.tagline: Measure how far the camera moved so her motion is read in the world
modules.summary: The camera follows her, so on-screen movement shrinks or even reverses mid-jump-chain. This module measures the camera's movement from the scenery, so her world position is her screen position plus the camera's. It has a fast strip method (x only) and a sturdier foreground-patch method (x and y).
modules.details_md:
**Why.** In MapleStory the camera trails the character. A long walk can look like a short one on screen, and a
jump chain's on-screen x can even go backwards. The platform she stands on scrolls 1:1 with the camera, so tracking
the scenery gives the camera.

**`camera_x(frames, rows, band=(12, 30))`: the strip under her.** It cuts the horizontal strip from 12 to 30
half-size px below her resting name tag (converted for the recording's geometry), converts it to grayscale floats,
and runs `cv2.phaseCorrelate` (with a Hanning window) between consecutive frames. Each frame's shift is rounded to
half a pixel (`round(dx * 2) / 2`) because the game scrolls in whole pixels (half pixels at scale 2) and rounding
stops sub-pixel noise from adding up into drift. Scenery moving left on screen means the camera moved right, so
the shift is subtracted. `world_x` adds this cumulative camera x to each row's tag x.

**`camera(frames, her)`: foreground patches.** The strip method fails where her own body or a drifting cloud is in
the strip, and clouds move on their own, so estimates taken over the whole scenery drifted. Instead:

1. `foreground` marks platform pixels: grass green (`g > 120`, `g > b + 50`, `g > r + 5`) or dirt brown (a band of
   red/green values with low blue). These are one map's colours.
2. `_patch_shifts` walks a grid of `PATCH` (24 px) squares, half a patch apart, and skips patches near her
   (`HER_BOX`: 40 px either side and 75 above her tag, `HER_BELOW` 22 below), patches that are less than 25%
   foreground (`PATCH_MIN_FOREGROUND`), and flat ones (std under `PATCH_MIN_STD` 15). Each remaining patch is
   matched in the next frame within `SEARCH` (10 px) with `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED`; matches under `PATCH_MIN_SCORE`
   (0.85) are dropped; the rest are refined to sub-pixel with `track.peak`.
3. For each frame step, the x shifts are binned to half a pixel, the most common bin wins, the patches within 0.75
   px of it are kept, and their median (x, y) is the camera's step. With fewer than two patches the camera is taken
   as not having moved.

All pixel constants are half-size px of the 1920x1080 window; `geo.ifpx`/`fpx` convert them. `physics_check` uses
`camera` (both axes); the `combo` analysis and the `track` command use `world_x`.

modules.title: Combo analysis
modules.tagline: Which way each jump and throw went, key lag, and frame pacing
modules.summary: Splits a recording of back-to-back combos into per-combo results: each jump's direction (back, forward, straight up) and each claw throw's side (toward the front or not). Also measures how late keys went out against the plan and the game's frame pacing. This is the original purpose of gamelab: checking MapleHelper's combo timing.
modules.details_md:
**`combos(rec, starts, end_ms, facing, template)`.** The `combo` command records several runs of a combo and calls
this on each recording:

1. Tracks her tag (`track.track`), turns it into world x (`scroll.world_x`), finds swings (`track.swings`) and
   airborne spans (`track.airborne`), all with the recording's geometry.
2. Cuts the timeline into windows from each combo start to the next (the last to `end_ms`).
3. **Jumps:** for every airborne span whose takeoff falls in the window, `dx` is world x at landing (or the last
   frame) minus world x `TAKEOFF_LEAD_MS` (20 ms) before the takeoff was seen. If `|dx|` is under `UP_PX` (12
   half-size px, converted; a normal jump moves about 45-65) it went `up`; otherwise `back` if its sign is away from
   the way she faced at the first combo (`-directions.sign(facing)`), else `forward`.
4. **Throws:** swings seen from `SWING_SHIFT_MS` (300 ms) after the window's start to 300 ms after its end belong to
   it, because a throw's swing shows about 0.5 s after its key. Each is `toward_front` if its side is the side she
   faced (`'R'` when facing `RIGHT` from `maplehelper.engine`).

The `combo` command prints each combo's jumps and throws, flags any jump not in the allowed set or any throw the
wrong way, and totals them across runs (the runs alternate facing so she ends about where she started).

**`send_lag(rec)`**: for each planned/sent key event pair, how late it went out (sent ms minus planned ms): count,
max and mean. It "should be a few ms at most".

**`frame_pacing(rec)`**: a frame is a new game frame when its mean absolute pixel difference from the previous one
is over `NEW_FRAME_DIFF` (0.05). It returns the count, median, 95th percentile and largest gap between new frames,
and lists gaps over `LONG_GAP_MS` (45 ms). The `check` command prints both and notes that long gaps while she stands
still are only frames that didn't change.

**What these tools found** (the README's opening lines, gamelab's first purpose): a regular attack locks out jumps and attacks for about 730 ms (the `lock` command measures the jump side of it: an attack, then a jump `d` ms later, and whether `track.airborne` sees her leave the ground), and quick taps right after takeoff were missed about 6% of the time.

modules.title: Physics check
modules.tagline: Her tracked movement in 18 recordings against the motion models, as RMS error
modules.summary: Tracks her in saved recordings to a fraction of a pixel with the camera taken out, replays the same keys through three movement models, and prints each model's RMS error in map units, x and y. With --fit it also fits the engine's lags per recording; with --fixture it saves the tracks as test fixtures.
modules.details_md:
**Her measured track** (`tracked`). For a recording in `lab/recordings`, every frame is matched with
`track.fine_match` against her calibrated tag template for the recording's size, and `scroll.camera` measures the
camera from foreground patches (her place given as the tag's centre). Her position is `(tag + camera - first
position) * units_per_px`, in map units with x right and y down. The keys come from the recording's `sent` events,
named by her key bindings (`her_key_names`, from config.toml [keys] via `control.timeline.her_setup`). Frames whose
tag score is under `MIN_SCORE` (0.45) are left out (another name tag over hers, a blur). The `recordings` folder is
git-ignored, so `load` falls back to `tests/fixtures/tracks/<name>.json` (6 are kept: motion, walk, jb_k165, jb_k190,
jb_k450, held_jump).

**The models**, each given the same key timeline:

- **before** (`steps` with `BEFORE`): what the planner and simulator modelled before `motion.body`: standing, she
  runs at full speed `run_lag` (0.12 s) after the arrow; let go, she runs on, then brakes evenly; in the air her
  sideways speed never changes. Constants: walk 149, jump lag 0.055 s, 27 units run on after release of which 13
  braking.
- **steps** (`steps` with `NOW`): the same step model with today's constants derived from the thief's shoe (`SHOE =
  physics.shoe_of(thief.FIXED_STATS)`): its walk, `LAGS.on + vmax / (2 acc)` run lag, `physics.JUMP_LAG`, and
  `body.stop_distance` / `body.slide` for braking. This is how the simulator moved her until it ran on the engine.
- **engine** (`engine`): `motion.body.replay` with the median `body.Lags` (66 ms arrow on, 68 off, 65 jump), its
  path the mean over every phase the game's 30 ms steps can have against the keys (`body.phases()`: 0, 5, ... 25
  ms). That mean is what the planner's closed forms expect.

`errors` interpolates each model's path at the tracked frame times up to the case's `until` and returns RMS x, RMS y
and the model's last x. `CASES` gives each recording its compare-until time and any floor she lands on that isn't
her starting one (e.g. `chain` lands 60.4 units up at 0.6 s). The jump-backs end before they land, because an attack
then plays and stops her dead (slides of 1.4-2.9 units where braking would give 7.6-11.7).

**`--fit`** (`fit_lags`): for each step phase, coordinate descent over the engine's `on`, `off` and `jump` lags on
grids (5 ms steps for on and jump, 10 ms for off, 20-100/105/120 ms), 3 rounds from the medians, minimising x² + y²
error; the best phase and lags win. It shows what's left once the lags' spread is removed.

The printout is a Markdown table per recording plus means (and medians) over all, and a second mean without
`SET_ASIDE` (`do_ledge2`: moving camera at 30 fps, camera recovered only to about 15%, and its x errors dominate the
difference between models).

**What it found** (README, Motion planning: Fit): with the fixed median lags the engine follows the 18 recordings to 1.94 units RMS in x and 1.67 in y (medians 1.61 and 1.17; without `do_ledge2` 1.82 and 1.57), and with lags and phase fitted to each, 0.89 and 0.75. `tests/test_recordings_physics.py` asserts the engine beats `BEFORE` by more than 1.2 units in both x and y on the six fixtures (1.40 / 1.80 against 2.86 / 3.29).

modules.title: Walk fit
modules.tagline: Her real walk, climb, takeoffs, steps and arrivals against her planned walk
modules.summary: Reads any run's telemetry (the hunt's and the perception service's) and measures, per run and per map, her steady walk and climb, how late her takeoffs came, how far her steps went against what was asked, and how many 'arrived' trips ended on the wrong platform, all against the walk the run planned her moves at. Built after a run planned at 125 units/s turned out to walk 148.
modules.details_md:
**Why it exists.** Every timed hold she makes runs open loop on the planned walk (`motion.physics.WALK_SPEED`), so a
planned walk that isn't hers sends every timed walk too far or short. On 2026-11-02 RiceBaby was planned at 125
units/s and walked 148: takeoffs came late by about a sixth of the walk before them, steps went 1.19 times what was
asked, and 15 of an hour's 210 'arrived' trips had her off the end of the destination platform. It went unnoticed
from 10-29 to 11-02, and the scripts that found it were hard-wired to that day's files and to 125. walkfit reads
the planned walk from the run's own records instead.

**Reading runs.** `files_of` collects every `*.jsonl` named (folders, and a `telemetry/` folder inside them, as a
golden clip has), keeping the largest copy of each file name. Files whose session `command` is `perceive` (or
named `-perceive`) are the perception service's; tour/hunt/nav files are hunts. `_records` pre-filters lines by
text (`"topic":"scene"`) before parsing, for speed. A `Run` holds one hunt file's session, scenes, chains, trips (each
with the last look before it), stances and `motion` records, plus the service's scenes and `touch` events within
5 s of its span (each touch at its own moment: time less `late`). Without service records it uses the hunt's own
looks. `--frames` cuts each recording folder's span (from its `index.jsonl`'s first and last `at`) into its own run.

**The measures** (`fit`):

- **walk / climb** (`stretches`): `motion.steady.measure` on her places: stretches on one platform moving one way at
  a walk, run-up and braking tail (`TAIL_S`) left out, a line fitted, slopes taken out by the v83 rule where the map
  model loads. Without service scenes, consecutive looks may be up to `GAP_LOOKS_S` (0.6 s) apart. `--raw` gives
  the older measure (x speed with braking tail, no slopes). Reported: median, quartiles, standard error, n; the
  ratio to the planned walk; the SPEED it implies (walk / 1.25 - 20) and that minus her stat window's SPEED
  (`panel`, from 'motion' records, `--speed`, or the session's physics).
- **takeoffs** (`takeoffs`, `engine_residuals`): chains whose first leg is a walk of `TAKEOFF_LEAST` (20) units or
  more then a jump, untouched until takeoff; the takeoff is the scene pair where her mode goes ground to air, within
  `TAKEOFF_S` (4 s). How far past the planned takeoff she left (+ late), the median for all and for walks of
  `LONG_WALK` (100)+, a line `late = slope x walk + b`, and the residual against the engine (`body.run_time` at the
  planned walk, `body.run_x` at the measured one) using the planned walk as of each chain (`Run.walk_at`).
- **steps** (`steps`): 'stepping away left/right N' stances, untouched from 0.3 s before to 1.8 s after, on one
  platform, on the ground; gone = where she first stood still (moves under 2 units) against N, only steps she
  actually walked (no next stance record before she stood still, and gone the way asked). Ratio over steps of 30+.
- **arrived** (`arrivals`): trips that ended 'arrived' and whether her platform was the trip's `dst`, with and
  without a touch in the 3 s before.

**The planned walk** (`planned_walk`): the session record's `physics` (from 2026-11-02), else `--planned`, else the
`--character` profile as the code has it now, said to be an assumption. `fit_runs` fits each run, then each map with
several runs; `table` prints one line each with a legend.

**Run it** as `python -m gamelab.analysis.walkfit RUN [RUN ...] [--planned UNITS] [--character ID] [--speed SPEED] [--frames] [--raw] [--json]` (there is no `gamelab` command for it). A RUN is a telemetry folder or files; nothing here sends a key or looks at the game.

**Checked against the analysis that found the problem.** On R1-R3 of 2026-11-02 (`--planned 125 --raw`: they have no physics record) it reproduces that analysis to the digit (docstring): the hour's steady walk 148.2 over 81 walks, 18 of 210 'arrived' trips on another platform (15 with no touch), takeoffs +7.5 units late at the median and +24.9 after walks of 100 or more (108 legs). By the estimator (without `--raw`) the walk is 149.4 over 66, implying SPEED 99.6 against her stat window's 100.

modules.title: Route coverage
modules.tagline: Each route move planned, taken and missed, and why the unused ones lose
modules.summary: Tallies, from a run's telemetry, how often each move of the map's route graph was planned, taken and missed, where she spent her time and which platforms moves got her onto. Then, for every move never taken, it computes its cost gap to the routes chosen instead and names why it lost. Works on the simulator harness's runs and on live telemetry.
modules.details_md:
**Run it** as `python -m gamelab coverage [RUN ...] [--live] [--map ID] [--ways N] [--text FILE] [--picture PATH]` (offline, no keys): each RUN a saved harness run (`sim.harness.load`); `--live`, or no RUN, tallies the live telemetry in `lab/telemetry` (but the simulator's `-sim-` files), only the files of the map asked. Its picture: moves taken in green (thicker the more often), planned but never taken in yellow, never planned in red.

**The graph.** `Graph` wraps `motion.route.Planner` for a map: its `moves`, each keyed by `key_of` as
`"<kind> <src>-><dst> @<x>"` (e.g. `jump 32->29 @536`). `step(m)` is a move's planner cost (`m.seconds +
RISK[kind]`), `cost(moves, x)` a route's cost from x with walks at `WALK_SPEED` (no random weights, no penalties),
`via(m, src, x, dst)` the quickest route from a place to a platform that makes move m, and `chains(m)` whether
`motion.flow.Flow` can chain the move from standing at its start in any variant (None for rope climb-downs and rope
jumps, which only the mover makes). `graph_for` caches one Graph per process (0.25 s to build).

**One run** (`tally(records, graph)` → `_Tally`), record by record:

- `scene` and `glance` records give her places; time between looks is added to the look's platform (at most
  `GAP_S`, 5 s); a change of platform is a visit.
- `route` records count every move in them as **planned** (replans too). Moves are matched to the graph by kind,
  platforms and start x within `MATCH_DX` (3 units); routes recorded before 2026-10-21 (no `from`) were on an older
  graph and are matched loosely to the nearest. Each fully matched route becomes a **plan**: from where (rounded to
  `PLAN_DX` 5), to which platform, its cost, the quickest cost, and what it kept off / avoided.
- `moved` records (the navigator's own, from 2026-10-21) give each chain's legs, where she landed, and whether she
  was hit. Before them, `chain` records and the navigator's log lines are parsed with regexes (`_ALONE`,
  `_ELSEWHERE`, `_CUT`).
- `_outcome` decides which leg failed: `stood` turns her places into the platforms she stood on (on a surface within
  `STAND_DX`/`STAND_DY` 6 units, `STAND_N` 2 times in a row), and `follow` walks them along the chain's platforms.
  Legs before the failure are **taken** and count as arrivals; the failed leg is **missed** (with where she ended)
  or a **hit's** (a hit on the way that left her elsewhere); legs after it weren't reached.
- `trip`, `tour` and `hunt` records give trip results (and trips with no route: timeouts before she set off), the
  tour's stops and the hunt loop's grounds.

The result is plain JSON (3-7 KB a run, README); the harness stores one per run and `merge` adds them up,
re-keying moves to today's graph (`rekey`).

**Why moves lose** (`report`). `map_wide` tries starts every `START_STEP` (60) units along every platform to every
other platform and finds the least each move adds to the quickest route. `plan_gaps` checks every move against the
plans actually made: on plans that kept nothing off and avoided nothing, how many could have used it, the least gap,
how many had it within `VARIETY` (route.NOISE, 35%) of the chosen route, and how many had it cheaper; on penalised
plans, whether a cheaper route through it hit what they kept off. `why` then picks, in order: **replanned** (planned
but replanned before she got there), **then** (cheaper today but planned on an older graph), **weights** (cheaper:
the random 1-1.35 weights drew another), **penalty**, **nowhere**, **cost** (never within 0.05 s of quickest
anywhere), else **ground** (quickest somewhere, but no trip went there). `drawn` simulates the navigator's random
weights (`DRAWS` 40 a plan, or `WAY_DRAWS` 8 with `route.ROUTES` > 1 using `route.chances`) to estimate how often
they'd send her through a move. On the first map the report adds platform 12 and the 23 -> 17 rope hops.

`picture_rows` gives (move, planned, taken) for `ui.render.coverage_picture`.

**What it found** (README, Route coverage, 2026-10-21, the first map): 204 moves in the graph; the simulator's hunts hardly left the basin (the hunt loop spent 87.5% of its time on platform 36, live 17.4%), and of the moves never taken most lost to where the trips went ('ground': the tour's 72 of 106, the loop's 137 of 159), not to their cost.

modules.title: Respawns and drop life
modules.tagline: How soon emptied platforms refill, how long drops lie, how full platforms are
modules.summary: From telemetry, measures three things as survival estimates over censored observations (Kaplan-Meier): the time from a kill that empties a platform until a monster is seen there again, how long a drop lies before it vanishes without her picking it up, and how full the spawn platforms are while in view. Its 2026-10-21 results are why behavior.hunt's and sim.world's RESPAWN stayed at 8 s, their comments quoting what it measured.
modules.details_md:
**Run it** as `python -m gamelab respawn [FILES ...] [--map ID] [--text FILE]` (offline, no keys): by default the live telemetry but the simulator's files, each file only if its session is on the map asked. The command hands in what this layer may not import: `localization.pose.Camera(model.bounds).corner`, the band (`attack.reach.LOOK_UP`, `LOOK_DOWN`), whether a probe run looks wide (`behavior.probe.PROBES`), and the map's cached game data for `spawn_fields`.

**Which looks count** (`looks`, `covers`). A look can say a platform is empty only if it searched for monsters
with her standing, and all of the platform was in the searched area: her band (`band` = attack.reach's LOOK_UP above
her feet to LOOK_DOWN below, a monster's body `BODY` 60 units tall fitting in it) or, for a whole-screen look, the
screen above the bottom bar and clear of the minimap, less `EDGE` (40 units) at each side. From 2026-10-21's evening
each scene record says whether it searched, whether wide, where it looked for drops, the view, and whether she
stood. For older records these are inferred: a look searched if it saw a monster, if a 'monsters' or 'stance'
record followed it, in a probe's run off a trip, or in `watch`; she stood if her tag was on her platform's surface
(`STAND_DY` 6) and not within `AIR_S` (1.3 s) of a jump stance. The view comes from the camera model passed in
(`localization.pose.Camera.corner`).

**(a) Respawn episodes** (`respawns`, `_episode`). A kill (hers from 'kill' events; others' from the feed's 'died'
events) starts an episode only if a monster of its kind was seen within `KILL_DX` (60) of it in the `KILL_SEEN_S`
(3 s) before. From `FADE_S` (1.5 s) after (a dying monster is seen for up to 1.26 s), covering looks must see the
platform empty `EMPTY_N` (2) times, `EMPTY_S` (0.5 s) apart. A monster then seen there (or another kill there) ends
it at the midpoint between that look and the last empty one, if they're at most `MAX_GAP` (2 s) apart; a longer gap
censors it at the last empty look ('away'), as does the run's end or `HORIZON` (180 s). A monster first seen with an
HP bar was hidden under damage numbers and drops the episode. Episodes are also split into **lone** (no other kill
there in `LONE_S` 15 s) and **near** (her within `NEAR` 150 units of a spawn point).

**(b) Drop life** (`drops`, `_gone`). Drops are told apart by kind and place (`DROP_DX` 8 units). A drop is born at
a kill of hers within `LOOT_REACH` (60) and `BIRTH_S` (20 s) before it was first seen ('hers'), else when first seen.
It's gone when two looks `EMPTY_LOOKS` (1.5 s) apart that looked where it lies, with her standing, inventory not full
(or it's mesos) and no other drop within `OVERLAP_DX` (15), don't see it. If she passed within `PICK_DX` (25) since
it was last seen, it's taken as picked up (censored). A later kill by it ends following it ('a kill by it').

**(c) How full** (`occupancy`). For each spawn platform, over covering looks (each weighted by time to the next,
`OCCUPANCY_GAP_S` 1 s at most): seconds covered, monster-seconds, seconds empty.

**The estimator** (`km`, `quantile`, `summary`). Kaplan-Meier with Greenwood's variance; 95% intervals on the
log-log scale (`Z` 1.959964); the median's interval by Brookmeyer and Crowley (as R's survfit gives it). Times and
shares left at `AT` (5 to 180 s, including MeowDB's 12.56 s) are given only where `MIN_FOLLOWED` (5) were still
followed.

**What it found** (README, 2026-10-21, 72 live files): of 77 episodes 12 were seen back, all within 10.8 s; 80% were
not back by 12.56 s, where the simulator refilled within seconds. Spawn points were 26% occupied while in view.
Drop life was over a minute (95% still lying at 60 s). The constants stayed: RESPAWN 8 s, DROP_LIFE 90 s (hunt) / 180 s (world). `hunt.DROP_LIFE` has since gone: from 2026-10-30 the hunt judges whether a pile still lies by `behavior.ledger.SURVIVAL`, fitted from the perception service's records, not by this report.

modules.title: Jump attacks and their jitter
modules.tagline: What came of each jump attack, and whether its key jitter predicts a hit
modules.summary: Reads a run's telemetry and gives each jump attack an outcome: a kill (an EXP gain naming its target came 0.1-0.85 s after the attack key), a hit (the target's HP bar dropped within 1.4 s), or nothing seen. Since 2026-11-01 jump attack keys carry a small random jitter; it tabulates outcomes by jitter bin and runs a stratified permutation test of whether jitter predicts a hit.
modules.details_md:
**Inputs.** 'jump' records (`behavior.fight.log_jump`, one per jump throw or jump back: `kind` why ('above',
'reach', 'passing', 'close', ...), `jump` ('up', 'forward', 'back'), `key_ms`, target, platform, x, dx, up, and from
2026-11-01 `base_ms`, `jitter_ms`, `window`, `turn`, `sure`, `n`), 'attack' records, 'jump_keys' records (whether
the keys went, `pressed_ms` as the player pressed them), 'exp' gains, 'scene' looks, and in simulated runs
'sim_attack' records (the world's own outcome).

**Outcomes** (`outcomes`):

1. `keys_of` lists every attack's key time (an 'attack' record within 0.1 s after a 'jump' gets the jump's `key_ms`
   added) with its target kind.
2. `kills_of` credits each EXP gain naming a kind to the latest attack at that kind keyed `KILL_AFTER` (0.1-0.85 s)
   before it. Live, a kill's gain showed 0.15-0.46 s after the throw's key (the server's), before the star even
   left.
3. Otherwise a **hit** if a look within `HIT_S` (1.4 s) after the key saw a monster of the target's kind on its
   platform within `NEAR` (60 units) of where it was, with an HP bar lower than the last look before the key had
   it (or newly shown). Else **nothing seen** (a miss, a star stopped, a hit hidden under damage numbers, or a
   monster already dead).

`service_records` prefers the perception service's own `*-perceive.jsonl` in the same folder when it covers the
run: its gains don't lag (the hunter's lagged by more than 0.5 s for 38% of kills live) and its scenes come 10 a
second (the hunter's looks between her keys missed a hit). `table` prints counts by why and jump kind, with
outcomes, the median attack key and the targets' median height.

**The jitter report** (`jitter_report`, `python -m gamelab jitter`). `jitter_rows` joins each 'jump' record to the
first 'jump_keys' record after it with the same `n` (`_keys_of_jumps`), takes the outcome from 'sim_attack' (the
first jump throw/back keyed within `MATCH_S` 1.5 s) in simulated runs or from `outcomes` otherwise, and computes
`pressed_jitter` (press minus base) and `otherwise` (pressed more than `PRESS_OFF_MS` 5 ms off the key sent, as when
a turn in the air was keyed differently; not counted).

modules.title: Look benchmark
modules.tagline: Time each stage of a look on saved frames or live, touching no window
modules.summary: Times every stage of a look (capture, HP bars, name tag, ground, minimap dots, ropes, EXP number, Lie Detector check, monsters) on saved screenshots or on the live game, and times DXGI against mss capture. Its SavedEyes, the real Eyes fed from saved frames, is also how other offline tools look at saved frames.
modules.details_md:
**Saved frames as a screen.** `load` reads saved screenshots (default `FRAMES`: 17 1920x1080 shots of her on
Thicket Around the Beach II in `gamelab/lab`, with monsters, ropes and drops in view), checks they are all one known
size (`screen.LOOK_SCALES`: 1920x1080 or 1366x768), optionally shrinks them (`--shrink 1366x768`, OpenCV area
average), and converts each to the BGRA picture a screen capture gives. `SavedScreen` and `SavedShot` stand in for
`capture.Grabber` and its shots, so `SavedEyes` (a subclass of `perception.eyes.Eyes`) runs exactly the same
conversion and look code as the game's eyes, with no window touched: `_to_front` does nothing, the client area is the
frame, and the window checks return none (the frame's own `framecheck` checks still run, unless the frames were
resampled). It takes the map's minimap picture, without which her dot would be read with the first map's origin and
`Senses` would refuse every look.

**Live, read-only.** `FrontEyes` raises `BadLook` if the game isn't already in front; it never brings it forward, so
it can run while someone plays.

**`Timer`** collects named samples (`time`, `add`) and counts; `table` prints n, median, 90th percentile and
fastest in ms.

**`stages`** times, on what the eyes capture now: the capture (and, live, the frame's age), HP and MP bars, the
half-size look frame, the name tag (near where she was and over the whole play area), the ground under her, her
minimap dot and other players', ropes over the whole screen and only where the map's ropes can show (counting ropes
the narrow search missed), the EXP number box and its read, the player's Lie Detector check, a glance, `Eyes.look`,
and the monsters in her band, on the whole screen, and each monster's HP bar.

**`run`** times the stages plus caller-supplied whole looks (the `bench-look` command passes `Senses.look` variants
and the continuous feed's step): on each saved frame `reps` times (default 5), or on `n` live captures (default 100).
The first look of each frame or run isn't timed (it loads templates and starts threads).

**`refused`** lists the saved frames whose looks fail their checks (framecheck, or a `Senses.place` refusal) before
timing: a look through Senses at a refused frame would retry for `senses.LOST_S` and then stop the command.

**`capture_stages`** (for `bench-capture`) times a look's full capture and a glance (minimap and the HP bar row)
through DXGI and mss on the same screen box, and counts whether the two see identical pixels. The docstring notes
offline numbers leave out the grab itself: mss waits for the compositor's next frame (16.7 ms), DXGI for the screen's
next frame, plus about 2 ms to copy 1920x1080 off the graphics card.

modules.title: Monster bodies check
modules.tagline: Where the detector puts monsters' feet, and how steady their x is
modules.summary: Checks the monster detector offline three ways: monster feet against the platform surface on saved screenshots; how much a monster's x strays frame to frame in recordings, whether it faces the way it moves, and whether its matched pose matches what it does; and the continuous feed's track velocities in `watch` telemetry.
modules.details_md:
**Feet on saved screenshots** (`feet_rows`, `feet_table`). For each monster a placed look put on a platform, the
feet's map y minus the platform's surface at that x (+ is below), measured two ways: by the template's bottom (as
before the templates knew where the feet are) and by the template's origin (`mob.feet`). Results are grouped as the
game's sprites together and each screenshot cut-out on its own (`is_cutout`: a template name ending in a number).
Screenshots where she isn't standing are left out (`AIRBORNE`, and looks whose scene isn't grounded): her own height
then shifts every monster seen (in `closeup.png` her tag is 9 px above where she stands and every monster reads 5-15
units low).

**x frame to frame on recordings** (`recording`). The detector runs on every frame of a recording with the camera
still (she stands). `link` follows detections: each live track takes the nearest detection of its kind within
`LINK_PX` (12 across, 10 down, converted) at most `LINK_GAP` (3) frames later. For tracks of at least `MIN_TRACK`
(15) detections, `residuals` measures how far each x is from a straight line fitted through the detections within
`FIT_S` (0.3 s) either side (at least `FIT_MIN` 7), by the template's centre and by its foot x. From the same local
slope (in units/s):

- **speed**: over `MOVING` (12) units/s, its speed is collected per kind (the game data says 125 units/s for a pig,
  43.75 for a snail);
- **facing**: whether its facing agrees with the direction it moves;
- **pose**: walking (over `WALKING_V` 30) or standing (under `STILL_V` 8) against whether the matched template was a
  'move' or 'stand' frame, by cut-outs and sprites.

`_spread` reports rms, 95th percentile and max in map units. `_slope` is least squares by hand, because
`numpy.linalg` killed the process with MKL until 2026-10-24.

**The feed's tracks** (`tracks_lines`). From `watch`'s telemetry 'tracks' records (twice a second): for each live
track seen in two records 0.3-1.5 s apart, its velocity against how far its x actually went: standing ones (under
8 units/s) should have |vx| under 15; walking ones (over 30) should have vx the same sign and within 30 units/s.

**Why.** The docstring's evidence: in recordings at 30-60 frames a second a monster's x jumped up to 10 units
between frames as the winning template changed from a sprite to a cut-out whose picture is off-centre.

`run` puts it together; the `bodies` command defaults to bench's saved frames and the `stand_snail` and
`walk_snail` recordings, each recording read at its own geometry (`recordings.file_geometry`).

modules.title: Pasted sprites benchmark
modules.tagline: Draw the game's own sprites onto frames at known places, then look for them
modules.summary: Builds synthetic test scenes: the game's own monster and drop pictures alpha-blended onto real 1366x768 frames at known places, exactly as the game draws them. The detectors then search the scenes at 1366x768 full size and stretched to 1920x1080 half size, and it reports what was found, how far off, at what score, how fast, plus how well a found monster is re-found in its next frame.
modules.details_md:
**Why.** There were no frames of the game at its own 1366x768 with the first map's monsters on them, and the new
maps' saved frames show their monsters in only a few places and poses. Pasting the game's own pictures gives ground
truth: every frame of every sprite, both facings, at known feet positions.

**Drawing** (`paste`, `scenes`). `paste` blends an RGBA picture onto a frame pixel for pixel: colour where opaque,
blended by alpha where see-through, rounded. `scenes` puts `PER_SCENE` (6) pictures on each background, at random
places at least `GAP` (12 game px) apart, below `TOP` (40 px: the title strip and party HP box), above the bottom bar
(`HUD_TOP`), and clear of the minimap; it tries 200 random places per picture. Monsters drawn facing right are
flipped (the game's sprites face left), and their feet are computed from the sprite's origin in the INDEX metadata.

**Two sizes.** Each scene is searched as a 1366x768 look sees it (full size) and as the 1920x1080 window showed it
until 2026-10-23: stretched bilinearly (`stretched`) and shrunk to half size (`look_frame`). Positions found in a
look frame are mapped back to game px by the pixel's **middle** (`_game`: `(v + 0.5) * upp - 0.5`): by the pixel's
edge, the first map's feet found at 1920x1080 came out 0.27 units left and 0.19 up on average (160 of them), by its
middle 0.06 left and 0.02 down.

**Monsters** (`monsters`). Every picture of the kinds all detectors know (those with a colour gate), both facings,
drawn `each` (2) times in random order. For each detector: a whole-screen search (`detect_wide`) and a fight's band
around each monster's feet (`detect`); a find counts if it's the nearest of its kind within `FEET_TOL` (10 map units)
of the drawn feet. Tallied per kind (`Tally`): drawn, found, found in band, found as the frame and facing drawn,
found by a cut-out (which says no frame), feet errors, scores, missed names, and extra finds where none of the kind
was drawn. The backgrounds alone are searched too ('clean').

**Drops** (`drops`). Every drop picture of the map's kinds (and the coins' frames), each searched in a strip just
above where it lies (`ABOVE`/`BELOW` of its bottom, `STRIP_PAD` 40 units either side), as Senses searches a
platform. A find counts within `ITEM_TOL` (6) of the picture's middle; coins also check the right coin.

**Re-finds** (`refinds`). For each standing and walking sprite: draw it, find it in the band, then draw instead the
frame it may show next (`STEPS`: unchanged, its pose's next frame, standing to walking or back, a flinch) with the
feet in the same place, and call `MobDetector.refind` around it as the feed does each frame, with and without the
fallback to the kind's whole template set. `Refound` counts found again, feet within `FEET_NEAR` (1 unit), as the
frame drawn, fallbacks taken, and times each re-find.

`lines` and `refind_lines` format the `bench-paste` command's report.

modules.title: Lab disk usage
modules.tagline: What gamelab/lab holds, by kind, and what is due to be pruned
modules.summary: Walks gamelab/lab and sizes every file by kind (recordings, Lie Detector recordings, recent recordings, alarm clips, screenshots, telemetry, harness runs, golden traces, inbox/outbox, other). It only reads; it also asks each pruner what it would delete next, as a dry run.
modules.details_md:
**`usage(lab)`** walks every file under `lab` with `os.walk`. A file's kind is the `FOLDERS` entry of its first
folder under lab (`recordings`, `lie_detector`, `recent`, `alarm_clips`, `booth_unknown`, `telemetry`, `harness`,
`golden`, `inbox`, `outbox`), or "other" for anything else (the player's log, learned stats such as `shots.jsonl` and
`grounds.json`, templates, notes). Files at the top of lab are "screenshots" if they end in `.png`. Each kind is a
`Usage`: file count, bytes, and oldest and newest modification time. A file deleted mid-walk is skipped.

**`report(lab, now)`** gives the lines `python -m gamelab lab-usage` prints: the total, each kind's size, file count
and date span, then what each pruner would delete now, as dry runs:

- telemetry: `telemetry.prune(..., dry_run=True)`; the newest 2 GB (`telemetry.KEEP_BYTES`) are kept, in parts of
  `telemetry.MAX_BYTES` (64 MB), and none is deleted for its age; `lab-usage --prune-telemetry` applies it now;
- Lie Detector recordings: `lie_recorder.prune` with `lie_recorder.KEEP_BYTES` (10 GB) besides the one being written;
- recent recordings (`save-recent`'s: `rolling.RECENT_KEEP_BYTES`, 20 GB), alarm clips (10 s before each alarm to
  60 s after: `CLIPS_KEEP_BYTES`, 30 GB) and Truth Booths of unknown cause (the recorder's 5 minutes before each:
  `UNKNOWN_KEEP_BYTES`, 20 GB): `lie_recorder.prune` with those keep sizes, besides the next one saved.

It ends by saying the other recordings and screenshots are never deleted for you: they are measurement evidence.

**`size(n)`** formats bytes for people (`512 B`, `3.4 KB`, `1.3 GB`); `save-recent` uses it too.

flows.title: How a combo test is recorded and judged
flows.summary: The `combo` command plays a MapleHelper combo through the key player while recording, then reads which way each jump and throw went from the frames.
flows.trigger: python -m gamelab combo NAME --runs N --chain K (sends keys; needs the elevated key player)

steps.text: Asks `_recording_setup` once for the calibration at the window's current size and the crop to record (a 100 ms capture through the key player, no keys); then, for each run, builds the combo's key timeline, alternating the facing so she ends about where she started.
Finds her tag on that full-size frame with the saved template; keeps the stored crop if the tag is within TAG_SLACK (40 client px at 1920x1080, converted) of its spot, else crops around her.
Hands the timeline to the key player via control.client.submit; the player presses the keys and captures the crop; frames, times and sent keys come back and are saved under lab/recordings.
steps.process: the command and the key player

steps.text: Runs the four measures below on the whole recording, then cuts the timeline into windows from each combo start to the next and sorts the jumps and swings into them.
Matches her tag template in every frame: (t, x, y, score) rows.
Adds the camera's x (phase correlation of the strip under her) to get her world x.
Finds claw swings and their side; combos gives each to the combo whose window, shifted 300 ms later, holds it, and marks it toward the front or the wrong way.
Finds jump spans from her tag's height; combos classifies each by world dx: under 12 half-size px (converted) 'up', else 'back' or 'forward' against the first combo's facing.
Prints each combo's jumps and throws, flags a jump not allowed for that combo or a throw the wrong way, and totals them over the runs.

flows.title: How her recorded movement is checked against the models
flows.summary: physics_check turns each saved recording into a sub-pixel world track and compares three motion models' paths under the same keys.

steps.text: Reads her key bindings (her_key_names, config.toml [keys]) and, for each recording asked (default all 18 of CASES), its track.
Uses lab/recordings/<name>.npz if present (tracked), else the track fixture in tests/fixtures/tracks (only 6 are kept).
For a saved recording: her tag in every frame and the camera, turned into map units from where she first stood, with the keys sent.
Her tag to a fraction of a pixel in every frame.
The camera's (x, y) from agreeing foreground patches, so her position is in the world, in map units.
The old step model's path with BEFORE and NOW constants.
motion.body.replay's path with the median lags, averaged over the six 5 ms phases of the game's 30 ms step.
RMS x and y of each model against the track up to the case's until; printed as a Markdown table with means and medians.
With --fit: the engine's on/off/jump lags and step phase searched per recording, a fitted column added. With --fixture, save_fixture writes each track to tests/fixtures/tracks.

flows.title: How runs become the route coverage report
flows.summary: Every harness run tallies its own telemetry; the coverage command merges tallies (and live telemetry) and explains the moves never taken.
flows.trigger: sim.harness finishing a run; then python -m gamelab coverage RUN... [--live]

steps.text: After each simulated run, stores coverage.tally(records, coverage.graph_for(model)) in the run's result.
Reads scene, glance, route, moved (or legacy chain/log), trip, tour and hunt records into counts; _outcome finds which leg of a chain failed from where she stood.
Loads saved harness runs and, with --live, tallies each live telemetry file of the same map.
Adds tallies per set, re-keying moves to today's graph.
map_wide and plan_gaps measure each unused move's cost gap; why names the reason; drawn estimates what the navigator's random weights would do.
Rows for ui.render.coverage_picture, saved by default as lab/shots/coverage_<map>.png (-2, -3 for further sets).

flows.title: How telemetry becomes respawn and drop-life estimates
flows.summary: The respawn command reads each telemetry file of the map into looks and kills, builds censored observations, and summarises them with Kaplan-Meier.

steps.text: Loads the map, the camera's corner function and the shooting band, and feeds each file of the map to Runs.add.
Per file: looks, kills, then the three measures; adds them to the running totals.
Each scene record placing her becomes a Look with what it searched, recorded or inferred.
Her 'kill' events and the feed's 'died' events (others' kills only where the feed ran) become Kills.
Each kill whose monster was seen just before becomes an Episode (or a reason it doesn't): emptied by two covering looks, ended by a monster seen back, or censored at a gap over 2 s.
Each drop becomes a DropLife: gone, picked, unseen, or cut short by a kill by it.
Seconds covered, monster-seconds and empty seconds per spawn platform.

Prints each set of observations through summary (km, quantile and survival: n, median with its 95% interval, quartiles, the share left at 5-180 s where at least 5 were followed), then occupancy per spawn platform.

not_done: Respawn on the first map (2026-10-21 data): whether a platform she empties refills by a delay at the spawn point or by a map-wide cap wasn't settled and the median isn't reached, so `behavior.hunt.RESPAWN` stays an unmeasured 8 s until an in-game check (its comment). Tree Dungeon's respawn was measured later (2026-10-29/30: the map's own tick, `sim.world.TICK_S` 7.115 s, filling it to a cap) with scratch scripts on the perception service's telemetry, not with this report.

This report's drop life is only a lower bound (others' takes look like vanishing), and no hunt left a drop long enough to show the game's own; the README proposed a `watch` session with drops left lying. Her drops' life is now modelled elsewhere (`behavior.ledger.SURVIVAL`: at least 180 s, then gone at the server's next expiry pass; one live pass took drops 198-228 s old), not by this module.
Coverage: to check in game, the first live run with the new 'moved' and route records, by `coverage --live` (README, Route coverage).
Jumps: a jitter pattern in simulated runs is the simulator's model; only live grinds can show a real one, and the soonest key's small jitter needs many attacks.
walkfit: twin platforms read as 'elsewhere' in arrivals; runs before 2026-11-02 have no physics record and need --planned.

physics_check: the engine (30 ms steps) follows the seven 60 fps walks less well than the 5 ms engine before it did (1.64 units RMS in x against 1.17), the long ones ending 1.6-5.6 units short of where she stopped; most of it is the release's lag, and which lag to trust isn't settled: a recorded walk of a few lengths, let go at a known time, would tell (README, Motion planning: Fit; tests/test_recordings_physics.py).
scroll.foreground knows only one map's grass and dirt colours.
bench: offline timings leave out the screen grab itself (mss ~16.7 ms, DXGI ~2 ms copy plus waiting for the next frame); `bench-capture` times those on the live screen.
